description: Red Meridian is a team of high school students brought together by a shared passion for engineering, technology, innovation, and space exploration. We enjoy tackling complex challenges, exploring creative solutions, and applying our interests in science and technology to real-world problems.
summary: Red Meridian developed a 3D Martian navigation system designed to help future astronauts explore the surface of Mars more safely and efficiently. Focusing on Gale Crater, our system uses terrain and environmental data to identify potential hazards, evaluate surrounding landscapes, and recommend safer travel routes. By considering factors such as slope, elevation, surface conditions, and environmental risks, the system helps astronauts make more informed navigation decisions in unfamiliar terrain. Unlike traditional mapping tools, our project emphasizes hazard awareness and route evaluation rather than simply showing locations and directions. This is important because Mars presents numerous challenges to exploration, including unpredictable terrain, steep slopes, and limited environmental information. By improving how astronauts understand and navigate their surroundings, Red Meridian hopes to contribute to safer and more effective future human exploration of Mars.
details:
What exactly does it do?

Our program works by allowing users to interact with a 3D, game-style representation of the Gale Crater and Peace Vallis Watershed on Mars. Astronauts can select their current location and desired destination, after which the system analyzes the surrounding environment to determine the optimal route. It evaluates several factors, including terrain elevation, slope steepness, potential hazards, surface conditions, and weather patterns. Using this information, the program compares possible paths and identifies the route that offers the best balance between safety and efficiency.

As astronauts navigate the Martian landscape, the system provides a visual representation of the surrounding terrain and highlights important environmental information that could affect their journey. In addition to generating navigation routes, our program calculates the overall safety of different locations within Gale Crater by evaluating their environmental and geographical conditions. It is presented as a percentage, with 0%-25% is low, 25%-40% is moderate, and 40%+ being high. This allows users to assess whether an area is suitable for exploration, travel, and scientific research. By combining 3D terrain visualization, environmental analysis, and route optimization, our program provides astronauts with a more comprehensive understanding of their surroundings and helps them make informed decisions while navigating Mars.

How does it work?

Behind the scenes, our program uses a combination of geographical modeling, environmental data analysis, and an A* pathfinding algorithm to generate navigation routes across Gale Crater. The crater is represented as a 70 × 70 grid, with each cell representing a 1 km² section of terrain. Each cell contains several environmental attributes, including elevation, slope steepness, thermal inertia, dust coverage, geological composition, and scientific research value. Using these attributes, the program calculates a composite hazard score for each location, assigning different levels of risk based on the environmental conditions and whether the mission involves an astronaut or a rover. It then uses the A* pathfinding algorithm to evaluate neighboring grid cells and calculate the cost of traveling through each one. Depending on the selected navigation mode—Safest, Fastest, or High Science—the algorithm adjusts the importance of environmental hazards, travel distance, and scientific value to determine the most appropriate route. Once the destination is reached, the program reconstructs the sequence of grid cells that form the selected path. Separately, our Java-based visualization system converts geographical coordinates into 3D Cartesian coordinates, allowing landmarks to be positioned and displayed on a rotatable, zoomable representation of Mars.

What benefits does it have?

The Mars Navigator, which we developed, allows future space explorers of Gale Crater to be aware of their surrounding environment via an interactive map. Using real NASA data, the system shows a map of the area with terrain, possible threats, routes, and interesting science targets for astronauts. Currently, the navigator shows Gale Crater and important places such as Mount Sharp and Aeolis Palus. Moreover, the application presents dangers related to steep slopes, and dust. In addition to the distance between any points on the map, the system presents the possible threats at those points. Thus, with the help of the system, astronauts will be able to make informed decisions concerning choosing safe routes.

What do you hope to achieve?

We hope that our Mars navigator will allow future astronauts to safely explore Mars by using an interactive map that displays terrain, hazards, routes, and scientific targets. Currently, it is centered on Gale Crater and utilizes actual NASA data to identify safe routes, significant locations such as Mount Sharp and Aeolis Palus, as well as potential risks including slopes, and dust. In the future, we plan to incorporate live weather, automatic route planning that takes into account walking and rover speeds, offline use for crews without internet access, and additional locations other than Gale Crater, like Peace Vallis and other areas of Mars

In the future, our team will improve the application by adding real-time weather so that astronauts will be able to react to any changes in weather conditions during their travels. The development of automatic route planning based on the speed of walking and the rover, offline navigation, and coverage of additional areas, including Peace Vallis, and then not only Gale Crater but other places as well, will allow us to make the tool useful for everyday exploration and emergencies. All this will enable.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Java and HTML were the two main languages we used to code our program. We used HTML to build the layout and make sure the interactive map and controls actually showed up properly on the screen, while Java ran the logic, distance tracking, and route decisions in the background. Afterwards, we hosted all of the code onto GitHub Pages for it to be viewed.

Since we weren't super experienced with coding some of the harder pathfinding parts yet, we used Claude and Gemini to help us write and fix parts of the backend code when we got stuck. Even so, our team came up with the whole concept, did all the research on Gale Crater and NASA's Curiosity mission, designed the features, and tested everything ourselves to make sure it worked.
